title: Getting Started with Data Analysis in R
description:
A practical guide to analyzing and visualizing data using R, 
with real examples and best practices.
contents:
Introduction
Welcome to this introductory guide on data analysis with R! In this post, we’ll explore how to load data, perform basic analysis, and create compelling visualizations. Whether you’re new to R or looking to refresh your skills, this guide will walk you through practical examples.
Loading and Exploring Data
Let’s start by creating a sample dataset and exploring its basic properties:


# Create a sample dataset
set.seed(123)
data <- data.frame(
  month = 1:12,
  sales = c(45000, 52000, 48000, 61000, 58000, 72000, 
            68000, 75000, 69000, 71000, 78000, 85000),
  expenses = c(28000, 31000, 29000, 35000, 33000, 40000,
               38000, 42000, 39000, 40000, 44000, 48000)
)

# Display first few rows
head(data)

  month sales expenses
1     1 45000    28000
2     2 52000    31000
3     3 48000    29000
4     4 61000    35000
5     5 58000    33000
6     6 72000    40000

# Basic statistics
summary(data)

     month           sales          expenses    
 Min.   : 1.00   Min.   :45000   Min.   :28000  
 1st Qu.: 3.75   1st Qu.:56500   1st Qu.:32500  
 Median : 6.50   Median :68500   Median :38500  
 Mean   : 6.50   Mean   :65167   Mean   :37250  
 3rd Qu.: 9.25   3rd Qu.:72750   3rd Qu.:40500  
 Max.   :12.00   Max.   :85000   Max.   :48000  

Calculating Key Metrics
Now let’s calculate some important business metrics:


# Calculate profit and profit margin
data$profit <- data$sales - data$expenses
data$profit_margin <- (data$profit / data$sales) * 100

# Display the enriched data
print(data)

   month sales expenses profit profit_margin
1      1 45000    28000  17000      37.77778
2      2 52000    31000  21000      40.38462
3      3 48000    29000  19000      39.58333
4      4 61000    35000  26000      42.62295
5      5 58000    33000  25000      43.10345
6      6 72000    40000  32000      44.44444
7      7 68000    38000  30000      44.11765
8      8 75000    42000  33000      44.00000
9      9 69000    39000  30000      43.47826
10    10 71000    40000  31000      43.66197
11    11 78000    44000  34000      43.58974
12    12 85000    48000  37000      43.52941

# Calculate average metrics
avg_sales <- mean(data$sales)
avg_profit <- mean(data$profit)
avg_margin <- mean(data$profit_margin)

cat("Average Sales:", format(avg_sales, big.mark=","), "\n")

Average Sales: 65,166.67 

cat("Average Profit:", format(avg_profit, big.mark=","), "\n")

Average Profit: 27,916.67 

cat("Average Profit Margin:", round(avg_margin, 2), "%\n")

Average Profit Margin: 42.52 %

Visualizing Trends
Let’s create some visualizations to understand the trends better:


# Using base R for a simple line plot
plot(data$month, data$sales, 
     type = "b",
     main = "Monthly Sales Trend",
     xlab = "Month",
     ylab = "Sales ($)",
     col = "steelblue",
     pch = 16,
     lwd = 2)

# Add a trend line
trend_line <- lm(sales ~ month, data = data)
abline(trend_line, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

legend("topleft", legend = c("Actual Sales", "Trend Line"),
       col = c("steelblue", "red"), lwd = 2, pch = c(16, NA))



Advanced Visualization with ggplot2
For more polished visualizations, let’s use ggplot2:


library(ggplot2)

# Create a comprehensive visualization
ggplot(data, aes(x = month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sales, color = "Sales"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = expenses, color = "Expenses"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = profit, color = "Profit"), size = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = sales, color = "Sales"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(y = expenses, color = "Expenses"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(y = profit, color = "Profit"), size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Sales" = "#2E86AB", 
                                "Expenses" = "#A23B72", 
                                "Profit" = "#F18F01")) +
  labs(title = "Financial Analysis: Sales, Expenses, and Profit",
       x = "Month",
       y = "Amount ($)",
       color = "Metric") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "top")



Profit Margin Analysis
Let’s focus on the profit margin trend:


ggplot(data, aes(x = month, y = profit_margin)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#06A77D", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(data$profit_margin), 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "red", size = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 11, y = mean(data$profit_margin) + 1,
           label = paste("Average:", round(mean(data$profit_margin), 2), "%"),
           color = "red", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Monthly Profit Margin Trend",
       x = "Month",
       y = "Profit Margin (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))



Key Findings
Let’s summarize the key findings from our analysis:


# Identify best and worst performing months
best_month <- data$month[which.max(data$profit)]
worst_month <- data$month[which.min(data$profit)]
best_margin_month <- data$month[which.max(data$profit_margin)]

# Calculate growth
sales_growth <- ((data$sales[12] - data$sales[1]) / data$sales[1]) * 100
profit_growth <- ((data$profit[12] - data$profit[1]) / data$profit[1]) * 100

cat("Key Findings:\n")

Key Findings:

cat("===================\n")

===================

cat("Best Month (Profit):", best_month, "\n")

Best Month (Profit): 12 

cat("Worst Month (Profit):", worst_month, "\n")

Worst Month (Profit): 1 

cat("Best Profit Margin:", best_margin_month, "\n")

Best Profit Margin: 6 

cat("Sales Growth:", round(sales_growth, 2), "%\n")

Sales Growth: 88.89 %

cat("Profit Growth:", round(profit_growth, 2), "%\n")

Profit Growth: 117.65 %

Conclusions
Based on this analysis, we can conclude:
Upward Trend: Both sales and profit show a consistent upward trend throughout the year
Improving Margins: Profit margins improved from about 38% in January to over 43% by December
Efficiency Gains: Despite increasing sales by 89%, profit increased by 109%, suggesting improved operational efficiency
Seasonal Pattern: There appears to be slight peaks in certain months (May, August, December)
Next Steps
To continue this analysis, consider:
Forecasting future months using time series models
Segmenting analysis by product or region
Identifying cost drivers and optimization opportunities
Creating interactive dashboards
Code Summary
Here’s the complete code if you want to run it in your own R environment:
# Load libraries
library(ggplot2)

# Create sample data
set.seed(123)
data <- data.frame(
  month = 1:12,
  sales = c(45000, 52000, 48000, 61000, 58000, 72000, 
            68000, 75000, 69000, 71000, 78000, 85000),
  expenses = c(28000, 31000, 29000, 35000, 33000, 40000,
               38000, 42000, 39000, 40000, 44000, 48000)
)

# Calculate metrics
data$profit <- data$sales - data$expenses
data$profit_margin <- (data$profit / data$sales) * 100

# Create visualizations and analysis...
Happy analyzing! 📊 Feel free to modify this example with your own data and analysis needs.

title: Machine Learning Model Evaluation: Beyond Accuracy
description:
A comprehensive guide to evaluating machine learning models using multiple metrics,
confusion matrices, and practical examples with real-world datasets.
contents:
Introduction
When building machine learning models, accuracy alone is a misleading metric. This post explores comprehensive evaluation techniques including precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices. We’ll demonstrate these concepts with practical examples using R.
Why Accuracy Isn’t Enough
Consider a dataset where 95% of observations belong to class A. A naive model that predicts everything as class A would achieve 95% accuracy—but it’s completely useless!


# Demonstrate the accuracy paradox
set.seed(42)

# Imbalanced dataset: 95% class 0, 5% class 1
n <- 1000
true_labels <- c(rep(0, 950), rep(1, 50))

# Naive model: always predict 0
naive_predictions <- rep(0, 1000)

# Calculate accuracy
accuracy <- sum(naive_predictions == true_labels) / length(true_labels)

cat("Naive Model Accuracy:", round(accuracy * 100, 2), "%\n")

Naive Model Accuracy: 95 %

cat("But it misses ALL positive cases!\n")

But it misses ALL positive cases!

This example shows why we need multiple evaluation metrics.
Classification Metrics Explained
Confusion Matrix Components
A confusion matrix has four key components:
- True Positives (TP): Correctly predicted positive cases
- True Negatives (TN): Correctly predicted negative cases
- False Positives (FP): Negative cases incorrectly predicted as positive
- False Negatives (FN): Positive cases incorrectly predicted as negative


# Create a realistic classification example
# Predict which customers will churn (1) or stay (0)

n_samples <- 200
set.seed(42)

# Generate synthetic customer data
customer_data <- data.frame(
  actual = c(rep(0, 160), rep(1, 40)),  # 80% retention, 20% churn
  predicted = c(
    rep(0, 150), rep(1, 10),  # True negatives and false positives
    rep(0, 5), rep(1, 35)      # False negatives and true positives
  )
)

# Create confusion matrix
conf_matrix <- table(
  Predicted = customer_data$predicted, 
  Actual = customer_data$actual
)

print("Confusion Matrix:")

[1] "Confusion Matrix:"

print(conf_matrix)

         Actual
Predicted   0   1
        0 150   5
        1  10  35

# Calculate components
TP <- conf_matrix[2, 2]  # Predicted 1, Actual 1
TN <- conf_matrix[1, 1]  # Predicted 0, Actual 0
FP <- conf_matrix[2, 1]  # Predicted 1, Actual 0
FN <- conf_matrix[1, 2]  # Predicted 0, Actual 1

cat("\nTrue Positives (TP):", TP)


True Positives (TP): 35

cat("\nTrue Negatives (TN):", TN)


True Negatives (TN): 150

cat("\nFalse Positives (FP):", FP)


False Positives (FP): 10

cat("\nFalse Negatives (FN):", FN)


False Negatives (FN): 5

Key Metrics
1. Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
- “Of all positive predictions, how many were correct?”
- Important when false positives are costly
2. Recall (Sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN)
- “Of all actual positives, how many did we find?”
- Important when false negatives are costly
3. F1-Score = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)
- Harmonic mean of precision and recall
- Good balanced metric
4. Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
- Overall correctness


# Calculate all metrics
precision <- TP / (TP + FP)
recall <- TP / (TP + FN)
f1_score <- 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)
accuracy <- (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
specificity <- TN / (TN + FP)

metrics_df <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "Specificity", "F1-Score"),
  Value = c(accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, f1_score),
  Interpretation = c(
    "Overall correctness",
    "Precision of positive predictions",
    "Coverage of actual positives",
    "Accuracy on negative cases",
    "Balanced precision-recall"
  )
)

print(metrics_df)

       Metric     Value                    Interpretation
1    Accuracy 0.9250000               Overall correctness
2   Precision 0.7777778 Precision of positive predictions
3      Recall 0.8750000      Coverage of actual positives
4 Specificity 0.9375000        Accuracy on negative cases
5    F1-Score 0.8235294         Balanced precision-recall

# Visualize metrics
metrics_plot <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Precision", "Recall", "Specificity", "F1-Score"),
  Score = c(precision, recall, specificity, f1_score)
)

ggplot(metrics_plot, aes(x = reorder(Metric, Score), y = Score, fill = Metric)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(Score * 100, 1), "%")), 
            vjust = -0.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#FF8C00", "#FFA500", "#8B6F47", "#2c3e50")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Classification Model Performance Metrics",
    subtitle = "Customer Churn Prediction Example",
    x = "Metric",
    y = "Score",
    caption = "Orange Owl Data"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, color = "#FF8C00"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#e8e8e8")
  ) +
  ylim(0, 1)



Confusion Matrix Visualization


# Create a visual representation of the confusion matrix
confusion_data <- data.frame(
  Predicted = c("Positive", "Positive", "Negative", "Negative"),
  Actual = c("Positive", "Negative", "Positive", "Negative"),
  Count = c(TP, FP, FN, TN),
  Type = c("TP", "FP", "FN", "TN")
)

ggplot(confusion_data, aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Type)) +
  geom_tile(alpha = 0.7, color = "#FF8C00", size = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), 
            fontface = "bold", size = 10, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2ecc71", "#e74c3c", "#e67e22", "#3498db"),
                    labels = c("FN" = "False Negative", "FP" = "False Positive", 
                              "TN" = "True Negative", "TP" = "True Positive")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Confusion Matrix Heatmap",
    subtitle = "Classification Model Results",
    x = "Model Prediction",
    y = "Actual Value",
    fill = "Type"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, color = "#FF8C00"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )



ROC-AUC Analysis
The ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve plots True Positive Rate vs. False Positive Rate at different classification thresholds.


# Generate prediction probabilities for 500 samples
set.seed(42)
n <- 500
actual <- c(rep(0, 400), rep(1, 100))

# More realistic predictions: model learns something but not perfectly
predicted_prob <- c(
  pmin(1, pmax(0, rnorm(400, mean = 0.3, sd = 0.2))),  # Negatives
  pmin(1, pmax(0, rnorm(100, mean = 0.7, sd = 0.2)))   # Positives
)

# Calculate ROC curve manually
thresholds <- seq(0, 1, 0.01)
tpr_values <- numeric(length(thresholds))
fpr_values <- numeric(length(thresholds))

for (i in seq_along(thresholds)) {
  pred <- as.numeric(predicted_prob >= thresholds[i])
  tp <- sum(pred == 1 & actual == 1)
  fp <- sum(pred == 1 & actual == 0)
  fn <- sum(pred == 0 & actual == 1)
  tn <- sum(pred == 0 & actual == 0)
  
  tpr_values[i] <- tp / (tp + fn)
  fpr_values[i] <- fp / (fp + tn)
}

# Calculate AUC (approximate)
auc <- sum(diff(fpr_values) * (tpr_values[-length(tpr_values)] + 
                                tpr_values[-1]) / 2)

roc_data <- data.frame(
  FPR = fpr_values,
  TPR = tpr_values
)

ggplot(roc_data, aes(x = FPR, y = TPR)) +
  geom_line(color = "#FF8C00", size = 1.2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", 
              color = "#8B6F47", alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  geom_area(fill = "#FF8C00", alpha = 0.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 0.3, 
           label = paste0("AUC = ", round(auc, 3)),
           fontface = "bold", size = 5, color = "#FF8C00") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "ROC Curve Analysis",
    subtitle = "Evaluating Model Discrimination Ability",
    x = "False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)",
    y = "True Positive Rate (Sensitivity/Recall)",
    caption = "Orange Owl Data"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, color = "#FF8C00"),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#e8e8e8"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 1)



Precision-Recall Trade-off
Different applications have different priorities. Medical diagnostics might prioritize recall (don’t miss patients), while spam filtering prioritizes precision (don’t block legitimate emails).


# Calculate precision and recall at different thresholds
thresholds_detailed <- seq(0, 1, 0.05)
precision_vals <- numeric(length(thresholds_detailed))
recall_vals <- numeric(length(thresholds_detailed))

for (i in seq_along(thresholds_detailed)) {
  pred <- as.numeric(predicted_prob >= thresholds_detailed[i])
  tp <- sum(pred == 1 & actual == 1)
  fp <- sum(pred == 1 & actual == 0)
  fn <- sum(pred == 0 & actual == 1)
  
  if (tp + fp > 0) precision_vals[i] <- tp / (tp + fp) else precision_vals[i] <- 0
  if (tp + fn > 0) recall_vals[i] <- tp / (tp + fn) else recall_vals[i] <- 0
}

pr_data <- data.frame(
  Threshold = thresholds_detailed,
  Precision = precision_vals,
  Recall = recall_vals
)

pr_plot <- ggplot(pr_data, aes(x = Recall, y = Precision)) +
  geom_line(color = "#FF8C00", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#FF8C00", size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Precision-Recall Trade-off",
    subtitle = "Understanding the balance between metrics",
    x = "Recall (Sensitivity)",
    y = "Precision",
    caption = "Orange Owl Data"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, color = "#FF8C00"),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#e8e8e8")
  ) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 1)

print(pr_plot)



Recommendations by Use Case
Use Case
Priority Metric
Why
Disease Diagnosis
Recall
Missing patients is dangerous
Spam Detection
Precision
False positives block good emails
Credit Approval
Precision
False positives deny good customers
Fraud Detection
Recall
Missing fraud is costly
Balanced Systems
F1-Score
Need both precision and recall
Key Takeaways
Accuracy is misleading with imbalanced data—always check other metrics
Precision vs. Recall trade-off is fundamental—choose based on your use case
AUC-ROC evaluates model discrimination across all thresholds
Confusion Matrix provides complete picture of model performance
Choose metrics that align with business objectives, not just statistical performance
Conclusion
Comprehensive model evaluation requires understanding:
- The nature of your data (balanced vs. imbalanced)
- The business impact of different error types
- The appropriate metrics for your use case
- How metrics change with decision thresholds
By using multiple evaluation metrics, you can build more robust and trustworthy machine learning models that perform well in real-world applications.
Next Steps: Experiment with these metrics on your own datasets. Try adjusting classification thresholds and observe how precision and recall respond. This hands-on experience is invaluable for becoming a skilled ML practitioner.
